utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Judge Agius is away on official business and Judge Stole is not able to sit with us on an urgent personal matter and therefore, Judge Prost and I have decided that it is in the interest of justice to continue sitting pursuant to 15 bis. I was informed that Prosecution has something to raise before we hear the next evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. We wanted to just raise one brief preliminary regarding the General Smith expertise issue that's been litigated to some degree thus far. It's the Prosecution's belief that the Smith expert motions and the filings thus far leave some issues open for in some cases further refinement, in some cases, with respect to some arguments, further elaboration. I think frankly some of the issues have remained a bit muddled and that's I think our responsibility as well as my friends' responsibility. I think I had just the way the motion practice has evolved on that issue thus far. It leaves a little bit to be desired in our humble opinion. We understand that oral argument is something that's not preferred because it takes away from court time, from witness time. We also understand that filing surreplies and motions for leave to file surreplies to surreplies is as distasteful for all concerned as is taking away valuable witness time and we want to avoid that ping-pong match, whether it's in writing or on our feet that Judge Agius referred to the other day. Nevertheless, we sincerely believe that the Smith expert issue does provide an opportunity for some limited beneficial oral argument on the issues that were raised. I've spoken with my friends representing Generals Miletic and Gvero about this suggestion. I think I'm batting about approximately 500 with them on whether they would agree to oral argument. I think it's fair to say that everybody on that side opposes a written motion for leave to file surreply and I think last I heard, one party would object to oral argument but would certainly be prepared for oral argument if the Court so ordered and one party does not have an objection to oral argument. We believe that some limited oral argument in total, 20 minutes, maybe half an hour, if there was some more back and forth, would be beneficial for the Court. We don't know where the Bench is in terms of its decision-making on the Smith issue, but if, in the next several weeks - that's usually the time frame with respect to certain issues being decided - we have a gap perhaps that opens up in the witness schedule, that might be a profitable way to use our time. All that said, I can represent to the Court that we will stand on the principle that I've articulated, although we believe that there are some issues that -- larger and smaller, that we would prefer to respond to or have the opportunity to respond to from the last filing from my friends, we will not move for leave to file a surreply to the filing. We will not do that. But we would like the opportunity to address certain issues, large and small, with the Court at the appropriate time. And I've also assured my friends that any oral argument we would not push for today or Monday. It would be in a sufficient time for everybody to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. I take it there would be no opposition from the Defence or -- Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Speaking on behalf of General Gvero, Your Honour, there is no opposition to this. That's right. Let me make it clear, we are not asking for oral argument but equally we certainly wouldn't oppose it. Could I invite the Chamber, informally, in effect, to make one precondition and that is that I and perhaps my learned friend Madam Fauveau have a further discussion with Mr. Thayer in which he could outline to us what it is that he proposes to say, because what we don't want to happen is to be taken by surprise by his arguments, so we have some vague idea what he's going to say. And we can prepare to respond accordingly and I would respectfully agree with him that half an hour should be ample to deal with the issue. As Your Honour knows from our perspective it's a very important issue and in some senses, whilst we don't invite it, we would welcome the opportunity for the Chamber to consider it more fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would very much encourage the parties to have a discussion prior to that. Yes. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to notify the Chamber that my position is a bit different. I personally am opposed to oral arguments. In fact, I'm not specifically opposed to oral arguments; I am opposed to the argument of the Prosecutor, to the reply of the Prosecutor. I would like the Chamber to comply by the rules and not to deviate from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give us one moment? My client wants to give us some instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, we have a small problem with the transcript. In fact, there is one whole sentence that is missing. I wanted to say that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence make it incumbent upon one party to make a motion, the other party to make a response and then the other party gives a reply. The rules of procedure do not give the other party to provide an additional reply. That is the Chamber -- that is the rule that I was concerned with, 126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Josse? Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Krgovic has spoken to General Gvero. We've got nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has the various submissions from the parties before it and the Chamber will consider the matter in due course. However, in the interim, as I said before, I'd like to encourage very much the parties to have the discussion among themselves. Let's bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just before you do I raised two preliminaries regarding to this witness a couple days ago when I thought he was going to start and I just wanted to remind Your Honours. I believe that a Rule 90(E) is applicable and also, the witness is literate but did not bring his reading glasses so he may not -- he may need to have the solemn declaration read to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is not because of his literacy but because of his eyesight?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is my understanding. He did not bring his glasses with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Before the witness is brought in, just one question from the Nikolic Defence. As was announced a couple of days ago, this Defence team is working on a submission that was announced to the Chamber and the Chamber granted a longer time for submitting this motion but we expect that the current version will be finalised today and we anticipate that the length exceeds the number of words allowed, 3.000, and we would like to seek approval from the Chamber to exceed 3.000 words so that the submission can contain everything that can be helpful to the Chamber to decide. I informed my colleagues from the Prosecution already and they do not object. Therefore, I kindly request your approval to exceed 3.000 words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It is so granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you didn't bring your glasses so that you cannot read letters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not. I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you give evidence here, you need to take a solemn declaration, so I will read out the declaration. Would you kindly repeat what you hear through the interpreters? I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One thing I would like to tell you, Mr. Djukanovic, is as a witness you have a right to refuse to make any statements which might tend to incriminate yourself. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, in some cases, the Chamber, the Trial Chamber, may compel you to answer some questions. However, testimony compelled in that way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against yourself for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I want to first say I'm sorry that you waited for some hours yesterday. That wasn't intentional on our part, to keep you waiting. First of all, could you tell us, please, when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of September 1914 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think there is an interpretation problem. Can I ask you again, sir, tell us when you were born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: 19th August, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Opravdic village, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Right now, in Opravdici village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, for the record, how about getting his name first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name, please, Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Milos Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And your ethnicity is Bosnian Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, earlier in my office, did you receive -- review and have read to you two written statements which you had given to the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you also listen to and watch your testimony from the case of Prosecutor versus Mitrovic and others in the BiH state court?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the village you live in, could you tell us where is that in relation to Kravica? How far away?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: It's two and a half kilometres from the school, looking from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us very briefly when and where you served your mandatory military service?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1961, I left on the 27th of March, and I returned on the 12th February 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you do that service?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first three months, I was in Lika area, in Croatia, and then I was transferred to the Italian border where my battalion command was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was in Slovenia, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what type of work have you done all your life? What's your occupation been?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've been a farmer and I did some work in construction, in the construction business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in 1994, were you assigned to any brigade in the VRS? Were you part of any military unit, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war began, I was mobilised into logistics until the 15th September or 15th August, I was in logistics. And then I was given labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you were in logistics, was that in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Bratunac Brigade. I don't know much about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in July 1995, were you performing your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, you mean 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls I'm sorry to interrupt you but I take it is 15th September or August in 1994 that he was demobilised? He didn't say the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was it in September or August of 1994 that you were then assigned to a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll ask you again: In July 1995, where were you performing your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was everywhere, mostly I was a repairman near Krajiska Oka [phoen]. There was a large agricultural estate where cows and pigs were bred. And then I went to do repairs in houses, wherever I was called, so I wasn't on that farm all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, which farm are you talking about that you say you weren't on all the time? Which village is that farm in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go now to Petrovdan in July 1995. Do you remember what day Petrovdan falls on?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know it's on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were you on the 12th of July 1995? What village?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember exactly. I think I was in Kravica on the 12th. I was in Kravica. I was minding the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as best you remember, the names of your colleagues who worked at this farm in Kravica or cooperative in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Zoran Eric. He was around me most of the time. And Nikolic also. We were working in the barn, working on a rota, and when we were free from that duty, we did other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember Nikolic's first name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Miladin Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now on that day the 12th of July when you were working in Kravica, other than the local villagers and the people working with you, were there any other people in Kravica, any strangers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some villagers around whom I knew. I still know them. They had returned to their houses. Elderly people, one or two per household.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were there any armed men? Any armed units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean armed men, apart from those who were standing guard or keeping an eye on things, I didn't know anyone, and I don't think they were from our area at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you their names or if you knew them, but who were these armed men standing guard who were not from your area? What was the name of their unit? How were they referred to by the people in the village?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard them referred to as specials or specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who did you -- who referred to them as specials or specialists, these armed men from outside the area?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly those who don't even know what a specialist is. How would I put it? I didn't know what they were myself. I just heard that name when people referred to them, and that's what I'm repeating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And these specials, where did you see them on 12 July 1995 in Kravica? You said they were standing guard. Can you tell me where -- where in Kravica you saw these men? Just describe that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In groups of two or three. Some of them were walking the asphalt road and some of them came into the perimeter. I didn't spend much time with them or talk to them. I just asked a couple of times, "Brave men, where are you from?" But nobody answered. Just one of them answered, saying that he was from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say some of them came into the perimeter, perimeter of what? What are you talking about? Where did they come into?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the perimeter of our cooperative, the farm, the perimeter formed by the buildings where we were accommodated, we who minded the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on the asphalt road you're talking about, is that the asphalt road that runs between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac and Bratunac-Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see any of these specials in the town, around the school?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That happened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What were they doing by the school, the specials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea what they did. I didn't go there. I just saw that they walked around there in groups of one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where is this school in relation to the farm in Kravica where you were working? How far away is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is maybe 700 metres towards Bratunac from the farm. I wouldn't be able to tell you the exact distance. It is probably between 700 and 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear, could we have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Something was missed there, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't heard the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, the last part of your answer was not caught by the interpreters. You said it's probably between 700 and 800 metres and I think you said. Can you just finish what you said next? Something about a road, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me about the road, towards Bratunac, where the school is. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could we have 65 ter 1563 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While it is being brought in, for clarification, you mentioned Petrovdan. It's St. Peter's Day, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we blow that up a little bit with the main buildings in the centre still? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, take a moment to look at that. I know you don't have your glasses with you. Can you just tell me what --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: But I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. What is that place you see in the photo? Where is that? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise it. This is the hangar. This is your barn. This is where we were accommodated, us who were tending to the cattle. And this is a building where offices used to be, or a kind of storage or warehouse or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The question was just that you recognise this then as the place you've been talking about, the farm where you were working on the 12th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with that for now. And could you please describe, as best you can, the uniforms you saw the specials wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were in one part, they were camouflage uniforms, a bit darker. They also had black belts, and they also had automatic rifles with folding rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, a while ago you said that they were guarding. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have one detail missing here. The witness used when describing the belts that the specials had, he said a word pleteni, and it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could ask the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you describe the belts, please? The black belts you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Black belts, around their waists, up to ten centimetres wide. In any case, they were not like we used to wear, they were not leather belts, they were knitted belts or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Fabric belts, is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Fabric, braided belts. I didn't pay too much attention. I did not hold them in my hands as to be able to tell what they were like. I just saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm just asking you to remember and describe things as best you can and you're doing fine. Now, you said these men were guarding. They were acting as guards, these specials. Who were they guarding or what were they guarding when you saw them on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who they were guarding, what they were guarding. I only saw them walking in groups of two or three on that asphalt road. They were within the perimeter. Sometimes they came up to us, they came closer. Nobody ever wanted to tell me what was being guarded, and I didn't dare ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you see any Muslims in Kravica that day? Any Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th? On the 12th, I wouldn't be able to remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Around that time, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, there were some who had arrived from the forest. They would surrender there and from there, somebody said that they were taken to Tuzla. As I was on my way to fetch water, I saw a man coming from the woods, and asked me where he could surrender, and I told him where to do that, and as I was walking towards the centre, there he was again and I told him, "You can go down there or you can go to the school." Actually, these were two different men. One went up to the farm and one went to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop there for a minute, please. So you saw two Muslim men that day who wanted to surrender and one surrendered to the school and one surrendered to the farm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you help that Muslim man, who wanted to surrender to the school, get to the school and bring him in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I only told him where to go, to the gate, to report there, because I'd heard that there was a bus there who was supposed to take everybody to Tuzla. It was parked there. That's why I told him to go either there or to go up to the school because there were buses there who were going to take them away to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember any specials saying anything to you when the -- at the school, when that Muslim man surrendered at the school in Kravica, asking you a question?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me whether I had searched him. I said, "Why should I have searched him? Who am I supposed to be to search him? Nobody ever told me that I was supposed to do that." And when they asked me what to do, I did it of my own goodwill because I meant to help them. For example, if I were here in a foreign city, and if I got lost and if I couldn't find my hotel and if I asked somebody and if they told me, I would take that as them helping me. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And when these two specials at the school asked you, they asked you if you searched the Muslim who was surrendering, did they ask you anything else? Or say anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask me anything. I didn't stay there any longer. I just brought the man to the gate. I had to divert for maybe 200 metres from my way, as this man had come out of the woods. One of them was actually wounded in the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which was the Muslim who was wounded in the neck? Was it the one who went to the school or the one who went to the hangar in the farm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The one who stayed by the farm, the first one, the one that I had encountered as I went to fetch the water. He was all wet, in jeans. He was holding his hand on his neck, and I realised that he was all covered in blood, and I heard from him that there are lots of them and they scattered through the woods, they didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again, I believe that one part of the witness's testimony didn't enter. I believe that I heard in our language that he said that they, meaning Muslims, had fought among themselves in the woods and I don't see that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what interpreter noted. Mr. Djukanovic, did you say that Muslims, they had fight among themselves in the woods? Could you repeat what you said earlier, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat. I heard that in the wood called Bokcin, as they were leaving Srebrenica, their commanders, one left them, the other stayed and they were all of a sudden two factions there and I heard from others that they had fought among themselves up there. That's what I heard later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Muslim you've just described who surrendered at the farm to the specials and went into the hangar, were there other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my intention to interrupt my learned friend but this is for the seventh or eighth time that the witness mentions the word "specials", the witness has never mentioned the word "specials". He said that they were soldiers and at the beginning, to my learned friend's question, how these men were called, he answered that people said that they were some sort of specials but nobody knew what a special was. I believe that it is in order to clarify that, the witness is using the word "soldier" and in the questions the word my learned friend keeps on repeating the is the word "specials" which may be rather leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I refer to your in-- draw your attention, line 10 of page 11, the witness specifically answered, well, I heard them referred to as specials or specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And the question was what was the name of the unit of these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic's microphone is not activated. Could you turn it off, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, it seems that my learned friend doesn't want me to speak. I apologise for the joke. This is exactly what I meant, on page 10 of the transcript, the witness repeated that that's what he had heard, that he heard these men being called specials but neither him nor anybody else knew what specials were. I believe that we should clarify whether we want the witness to use the word "soldier" as he does or "special", as the -- my learned friend is putting it to him. In the witness's vocabulary, I haven't heard the word "specials" mentioned spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what the witness has referred to. If you're not satisfied with the examination-in-chief, you can further pursue the meaning later on in the course of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Otherwise you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour and I would also ask that that type of objection in the future that he perhaps request -- that should not have been done in the presence of the witness. I could respond but I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the Muslim who surrendered to the specials at the warehouse and went into the hangar, were there other prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a couple in front of the hangar, standing by the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners total did you see around the hangar at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go closer. I stayed by the hangar corner. I saw some ten or 15 of them standing by the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the night of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, at one time the witness said that he went to fetch water. Could you clarify that? For whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I was -- we can do that now. I was -- that's sort of a chapter but we can talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, about why you went to fetch water and who the water was for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The one whom we called special ordered me to go and fetch water. I went, I found a plastic bucket of ten litres. I went to the well in front of Radoslav [as interpreted] Vasic's house. I could have gone to the river but I didn't. I brought this water to the hangar corner, and I passed that bucket full of water to him. That's when I saw some ten or 15 men standing there at the first entrance, in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the night of the 12th of July, into the 13th, do you remember what you were doing that night, if you had to do anything out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, nor what I did, but I know that on the 12th, I was by the barn tending to the cattle, and on the 13th, maybe in the evening but I don't remember the exact dates, I didn't pay attention to that, I didn't make any notes, I never knew that I would need all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- did you at any time during this period help to guard prisoners at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I didn't do this voluntarily. One or two of these policemen who were there, one evening, they forced me at 12.00 at night, as I was on my way to the barn to tend to the two cows that were supposed to give birth, they came my way, they commanded me to raise my arms, and I was with a colleague and they asked him to do the same and they forced us to go behind the hangar to a cornfield and they asked us to watch the windows, from there, from that cornfield. Later on, the director came and he saw us there, he stayed ten minutes, he went to his office, I don't know what happened next. We stayed there until 6.00 in the morning. When we wanted to -- when we said that the director told us to go to the cattle, to the cows, and then the director cursed our mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is again one correction for the transcript on page 20, line 15, it says, "one or two of these policemen". "Policemen". That's what it says here. And the witness never actually used the word policemen. I mean, I was listening in our language so the translation was not correct. He said one of these two men that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember what did you say in relation to the two men who forced you to guard the cornfield? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same ones that I referred to a little while ago. I don't know they were specials or not. I heard them being referred to as specials. But they took turns. Those who were there, up to 12, wore somewhat more modest clothes and those who forced us to watch the windows, they were a bit tougher. They were not the same ones as those before. They were not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said specials, those who were there during the day as well, those who were walking around. They are not -- they were not policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me read part of your statement to you that you gave to the war crimes investigators, just to see if it helps you remember the date where you did this guard duty. This is from the witness's second statement and it's paragraph 6. Page 5 in the English. "On the night of 12th to 13 July 1995, while I was in the shift with Zoran Eric, I set off to check on the cows in the barn around midnight, where we were intercepted by two very nervous special units members."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It then continues to discuss how they forced you to guard the prisoners that night. Does that help you remember whether it was the night of the 12th to the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was on the night between the 13th and the 14th. One day after the day of St. Peter. I really can't remember. It was 12 years ago and it's very hard for me to remember all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just refresh you with one other part of your statement. This is on page 55 of your testimony in the state court. At line 12 in the English. "From the 12th to the 13th, that means in the night of Petrovdan to the next day, that was most probably when these people forced to us keep guard." I'll ask you again if you recall that it was the night of Petrovdan into the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you that I cannot give you a guarantee as to what night it was, whether it was 12th to the 13th or the 13th to the 14th. I really can't be 100 per cent sure of that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you notice whether the specials had any shift changes during that time period, during the night?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was there between 12.00 and 6.00 in the morning, the same shift stayed in place, the same men were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you notice shift changes with the specials while you observed them around the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe let me put it this way: Do you remember any of the specials leaving and other specials coming to take their place? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: They probably took shifts. I didn't know them and I did not have any interest in observing whether they were the same ones or whether they were replaced by somebody else. I only saw them arriving in twos or just one of them and they would be walking on that asphalt road in groups of two or three. I did not have the time to stand and watch whether they were changing shifts or not. I did not even dare take a look at them at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just again try to help you remember this. This is on page 8 of your testimony. "I don't know if they were always the same men because they would relieve each other. I know the shift changed that night but I think it was after 12.00. It was other men. It wasn't the same men."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably weren't the same. They had a rota and the shift that took over at 12.00 was a different group of men. That's what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. While you were guarding the prisoners during the night, don't worry about the date, were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I had the rifle that was issued to me to stand guard at the building so that nobody could come and thieve. I had the PAP rifle, the semi-automatic rifle not only I, all the three of us; Miladin Nikolic, myself and Zoran had the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, besides you, as best you can remember, approximately how many specials were guarding the prisoners at the warehouse that night?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there were two or three of them together with two of us. I didn't go on rounds around the hangar to see who was there. I didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we please bring up 1563 again? All right. Take a look at that, sir, and what I'm going to ask is for the usher to help you to give you the special pen I told you about, and if you could please, if you can, look at it and mark where you were standing when you spent the night standing guard. Just put an X where you were standing guard.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the other side of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, then draw an arrow to where you were standing guard behind the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. My hand is shaking. It's on that side of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's close enough. The witness has made a mark indicating for the record his approximate location behind the hangar and could you just write your initials on the bottom right-hand corner, just write MD somewhere on there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Good enough.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: This part here, not the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, you just made a line in front of the hangar. What does that line represent?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: In this part here, there were those what do you want to call them, Bosniaks or Muslims. That's where they were. And the rest was machines that were burned down, trucks and tractors. This part here was not built up to the top. There was a procurement storehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just say for the record the witness made two marks in the field behind the hangar to indicate his position at night guarding the prisoners and he made two horizontal lines in front of the hangar closer to the asphalt road to indicate where he saw prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you see the prisoners, sir - you don't need to mark it - outside where you've drawn the line or were they inside the opening, the hangar we see there, or both?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the prisoners here in this part, next to the door, here somewhere, right next to the door, from this corner of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we can just save this as it is, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, could you write down your initials on the bottom right part of this picture, MD? Could you write down your initials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean where I was? Where I brought the water?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: What shall I write? What am I supposed to write down there? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: MD, M for Milos, D for Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And I'm finished with that for now. Thank you. I think we can -- I think the date is automatically recorded. I forgot to ask at the beginning, sir, I know that you have a bad back and it can trouble you. If you're in pain at any time while you're here, just let us know, if you need a break because you feel tired, a short break, just let us know. Would you like to continue right now or would you like a short break?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's continue so we can finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've talked about on Petrovdan, 12th of July, the people you saw and the specials. I wanted you to tell me about the next day. Did you see specials the next day, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers were walking around Kravica on the asphalt road, in groups of two or three. I didn't see any larger groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you see whether any more -- did you personally observe any more Muslims surrendering to the warehouse that day or being brought to the warehouse that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any. I saw only one group outside the hangar here. I didn't see if any more of them arrived because I didn't stand around all the time to see the comings and goings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about bringing some water to the prisoners because the one special asked you to. Do you recall whether you said anything to him when you gave him that bucket of water?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: When he ordered me to go and get that bucket of water, whatever you want to call it, I did that, and he was standing there with his rifle on his shoulder, and I told him, "Watch out. Somebody might snatch it away from you or kill you." And he said, "No. These people here are quiet." I went into the barn, stayed there for about five minutes and heard two short bursts of fire. I got out and then somebody told me, I don't know exactly who, somebody told me this special got killed, and one of the others got wounded, and I said, "That's impossible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, again, I believe that the interpreters didn't catch the last part of the answer of the witness. What we have is on page 27, line 7, the witness allegedly said when he heard about these incidents, "That's impossible." And basically what I heard him saying is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He would rather repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, when you heard about that event, you said, "That's impossible." And after that, what did you say? Did you -- could you repeat what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said the same thing and I have to repeat it. I didn't go there and I didn't see which one was killed and which one was wounded. I didn't go there at all. And everything happened the way I described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, maybe I was not clear enough. I never heard the witness saying, "That's impossible." I heard him literally saying, "I told him so. That's what I told him."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did you say after somebody told you that the special you brought the water to had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I said when they told me this special was killed, I said, "I had told him that would happen and he didn't believe me."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. After those two bursts of fire, what did you hear next? Did you hear any more gunfire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while I was at the barn, I heard -- I don't know how long it lasted. I heard a bit more shooting behind the hangar, but there was nothing around the barn where I was but what happened over there I don't know. I heard shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You heard shooting around the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the front part of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Approximately, best that you can remember, how long did that shooting last?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe ten, 15 minutes, but not throughout, not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Besides the shooting, what else did you hear? Did you hear any other loud noises?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard noises, explosions, but that was already towards dusk but I didn't go anywhere near.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you can tell, what do you think those -- what were those explosions from? What kind of explosions did they sound like to you, from being in the army and from being in this war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a bomb exploding, something like that. That's what I heard a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did it sound to you like hand grenades or like a different type of explosion, if you could tell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's all right. I didn't hear the other part of the question. Now I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did the sounds of these explosions sound to you like hand grenades, shellings or something else? What did it sound most like?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was like a -- more like a bomb rather than a shell.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Bomb could mean hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that we should establish first if the witness knows the difference between an explosion of a bomb, a grenade and a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I asked him that based on his military experience and experience during the war. And I had also meant during his service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "bomba"? What kind of device is that or explosive? When you say "bomba", describe what you're talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can describe a hand grenade or a bomb. You don't have to ask me about that. I know it. I went to the army; I threw hand grenades into a trench. The one with the security latch, the impact-activated one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said -- I think I'll move on. Now, after this -- hearing this shooting, hearing these explosions, were you able to see whether anybody had been hurt or killed from these shootings and explosions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I could see from that room I was in, from the barn, who was where and what they were doing. I was with the cattle in the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I mean after -- after this shooting and explosions, did you see anybody who had been hurt or killed around the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to get a bucket of water for us, I saw on the opposite side between the bus and the hangar, I saw a couple of dead bodies in a pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could we have the same exhibit, 1563, up again, please? Could you please -- the usher will give you the pen again. All right. Take your time and try to draw a circle showing where you saw these bodies after the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I draw my position? My vantage point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First draw a circle around where you saw the pile of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies? Here [Marks]. And I was here [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: And when I brought the water, I was there [Marks]. I mean while they were alive, while there were no dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So I think I will do it this way. The mark on the far left is where the witness states he was when he saw the bodies. The mark in the middle next to the corner of the hangar is where the witness brought the water to the special. And the mark on the far right is where he saw the pile of dead bodies. And if you could please -- at the bottom of the photo, write MD, please, witness.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So are you done with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how many specials, if any, did you see in that area, the area around the warehouse, at the time that you saw the pile of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three, were here on the asphalt road. I don't know if there were any more further up. There was a bus standing outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not quite time but I would prefer to take the break now, if it's all right with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Although the examination-in-chief hasn't been completed, can I confirm with the Defence counsel as to their time for cross-examination, for the sake of planning of the day? Is there any change?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe we will probably have no questions for this witness so that would be a change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Miletic will have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will not cross-examine this witness, very likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will probably have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we announced one hour, but in view of the examination-in-chief, we'll take less time, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I confirm with Gvero team that there will be no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is almost certain that we will have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we should have the next witness ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, we'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we talked earlier about the uniforms you saw the specials wearing, one piece with the belt. Were you able to see any kind of insignia, patches, any other special markings on the uniforms that you saw the specials wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any patches. I wasn't interested in them. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you also said you didn't know where these specials were from other than the one who told you -- did you see any of them in different --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: One said he was from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Did you see any of them wearing different uniforms that would show different ranks or anything like that or were they all wearing identical uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Those whom I saw all wore the same uniforms, those who were in my vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So that was all the armed men from outside the village you saw those days were wearing that same uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms in one part, as I've told you already, with wide [Realtime transcript read in error "white"] black belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think is it white or wide black belts? You said wide before?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Wide, the interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Black belts, ten centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My understanding is that it is only Mr. Stojanovic who will cross-examine this witness. Mr. Stojanovic is representing Mr. Borovcanin. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, good morning once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, let's just briefly take you back to your war path, so to call it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you joined the Republika Srpska army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of your unit during the first period of war was Milisav Obackic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the platoon commander, yes. Of the 2nd Platoon, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you referred to your unit as the Kravica Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what they called it. I'm not familiar with all that. I'm -- I was not interested in what platoon I was, what company it was. I know that I was in the rear all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were there up to August or September 1994 when were you given work obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that already in June 1992, at the beginning of the war, in your village, Kravica, several villagers were ambushed and killed, among them were Milutin Milosevic and Bogoljub Eric and others; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, of course I am. That was in my neighbourhood, very close to where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bogoljub Eric, was he the father [as interpreted] of Zoran Eric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've just been warned about the transcript. Was Bogoljub Eric grandfather of Zoran Eric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Bogoljub was Zoran Eric's father. He was elderly. That's why you referred to him as grandfather but he was his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also, you were in Kravica on the 7th of January 1993 on Christmas when the BiH army launched an attack on that village?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at home when the village started burning. I was at home in the evening when the villages started burning. I didn't know anything. And I saw in front of my house people running, crying that the surrounding villages were burnt. That's when I left my house and everything burned down after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you could get to the relevant point as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just two more questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the BiH army attacked from the direction of Jezestica and Siljkovici towards Kravica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: From all three sides. The only side that remained passable was to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in 1993, on Christmas that year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, in 1993, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the population that had been expelled was settled by the football pitch in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in working on that pitch all the time, the Norwegians funded that or somebody else. The settlement is still there, the settlement that had been constructed for the refugees and expelled population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at an exhibit in e-court which is 4D107? While this is being brought up, let me just tell you that this is a document issued by the Ministry of Defence, the Bratunac division, dated 10 July 1995, and I believe that this will bring me to the relevant period, Your Honours. Mr. Djukanovic, I've been told that you don't have glasses and you won't be able to read.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've forgotten them. Don't have them on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will read the document to you. This is a document by the Ministry of Defence, the division in Bratunac, dated 10 July 1995. It features a list of the military conscripts' files and these military conscripts were assigned to the work unit of the R Battalion within the Bratunac Brigade, and could you please scroll up a little? It says here that the commander of the 2nd Squad of the 1st Company, Milos Djukanovic, son of Rajko, born in 1940. My question to you is this: Do you know that already as of 10 July, you were assigned to the R Battalion on the strength of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there another person by the name of Milos Djukanovic, son of Rajko?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are several people by the name of Djukanovic but I was never a commander to anybody. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Next to your name, there is a handwritten word, sowing. Do you know that in that period, in July 1995, you had any duties in connection with this sowing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The interpreter corrects herself: It is not sowing, it is harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will go on and ask you this: On the 12th of July 1995, on St. Peter's Day, you found yourself doing work in the Kravica farm as part of your work obligation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived at that place, at the request of the then-director of the farm, whose name was Jovan Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you know Luka Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Luka Markovic very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those days, was he in any way your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was superior. I could never find a common language with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he give you tasks, orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did give me tasks, all sorts of tasks. He gave me all sorts of jobs, just to keep us busy, and when we were supposed to have a bite to eat he would go missing, he would just disappear, vanish. That's how it was. He was not a very nice person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you to put up a tent in front of the church in Kravica together with Zoran Eric?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Jovan Nikolic who ordered us to do that because we knew how to do that, Zoran Eric and I. We put up the tent but there was no celebration. On the following day nothing happened, no festivities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the farm in Ljubovija purchased a large quantities of drinks for the celebrations but they were not drunk, they were stored in the warehouse in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether the drinks were purchased or not. I really wouldn't know. Nobody ever told me that. And there was a storage, a warehouse, where I could go and I was in charge of but I did not see any drinks or anything of the sort stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you maybe hear that a warehouse, a farmhouse, was broken into and that a large quantity of drinks went missing on one of those days, either the 13th, the 14th or the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about these Bosniaks, Muslims, how you call them, who surrendered as they came out of the woods. Do you remember that you spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did one of them, to whom you talked, on whom you saw those injuries, tell you how he sustained them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk long with him, just exchanged a few words with him. He asked me where something was, I showed him the way, and the other one, I saw crossing the road towards the centre, he too was covered with mud, wet, soaked. I was smoking a cigarette. He said he hadn't had a cigarette in three days. I took one out and gave it to him to light up, although I didn't have many myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they escorted by any troops or were they on their own?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: They were coming down from the forest, less than 100 metres away, crossing the riverbed, going towards the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no escorts, no troops around them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One of them went towards the school?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I took one of them to the gate of the school because I was pouring water over there, the water supply did not work those days. I was going there anyway to get some water for us to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there was the kitchen and the logistics next to the school?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a kitchen there, right. Any one of the refugees coming by could stop and have something to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who held that facility? Whose kitchen was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain it to you. Whether it was a military kitchen or whether it was set up for civilians, I'm not clear on that. All I know is that our cook brought us meals three times a week when we were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you returned from the school, did you see outside the Kravica warehouse a military vehicle and persons who asked for a chain and padlock from Luka Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear and do you know that on that day, in fact during those days, a column of members of the BH army set out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla across the hills overlooking Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard people saying that those columns were passing, who their leaders were I don't know, and that they were supposed to meet at Bokcin woods and that they had -- there was some infighting among them and that some men got out of those woods injured, wounded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The stories went round, you run into one of the villagers, they would tell you. I don't know who they heard it from. At any rate, I didn't go up there and didn't see it myself so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If they were moving towards Tuzla, would you agree with me that there was no reason for them to go towards Siljkovici or Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that place where the woods are, from before, but when they came by that forest, they didn't know where they were. They could have known the neighbours who were from Kravica but those who were from Srebrenica didn't know the way and they didn't know where to go and that's how they parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you understand that as a movement on Christmas 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The same as we moved out of our villages on Christmas when they started burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I just noticed a bit of overlap with the speakers and I want the record to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the interpreters got it right but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think they did get it right but I thought I was hearing stress in the interpreter's voice a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you bear that in mind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm trying hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, please, you too try to wait a little when I finish my question before you start answering so it's all on the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you is that bus you mentioned. You said you had seen the arrival of the buses into the yard where the Kravica warehouse was. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was warned about interpretation, so I want to ask you was it one bus or several buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw only one bus. It was white. It is recorded somewhere that I saw a blue bus but that's wrong. It was a white bus parked there but what kind of licence plates, if any, it had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did that bus stand there before the moment when the shooting occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when the bus arrived, but I just asked, "What is the bus for?" And somebody said, "To take those people from the hangar out to Tuzla." But the bus eventually didn't go anywhere. It just stayed there, bullet-ridden.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago the bus was strifed [as interpreted] with bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you can remember, from what side was the bus strifed with bullets, from the warehouse side or?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, from the road towards the hangar when I went to get that water, and from the front side, as far as I was able to see, and it was standing outside the exit turned towards the east facing the door of the hangar. And after that I saw that pile of dead bodies that I saw when I brought the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us take it slowly, from the beginning. First of all, which way did the bus face? Did the front of the bus face Konjevic Polje or Bratunac, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you that, whether it was facing Konjevic Polje or whether Kravica, the east, I don't know. At any rate, it was strifed with bullets from the Kravica side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it just one side of the vehicle or the flanks as well that was ridden with bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see the flanks. I just could see the front side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was there any reason to shoot at that bus?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: What can I tell you? Maybe the reason was when that special, that man from the specials, got killed, and when the other one was wounded, the person who had shot them must have also shot at the bus, but what happened after the rifle was taken away from that person, the other special shot at that person. I saw -- in fact I heard later that the shooter himself was wounded but I didn't see any of it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say the person who shot at them probably hit the bus as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I imagine it. The person who shot at the special must have also shot in the direction of the bus, but who else shot from the other side, I can't tell you because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note Mr. Nicholls on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness previously said he didn't know and this was going to be pure speculation and my friend is asking him to speculate further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's right. Let's move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you were talking with this soldier, or that man from the specials, as you call him, and when he asked you to get water, did you at any time notice that the column of prisoners, Muslim prisoners, was entering the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that there is a version of these events, according to which the column of Muslim prisoners was entering the hangar and when the last of them was in, the Serb soldier hit him and opened fire and immediately after that, shooting started from all sorts of weapons, would you agree that that is right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there to see who shot at whom and I didn't see the column. I just saw ten or 15 of them outside the hangar close to the door, between 10 and 15. I cannot guarantee how many exactly. And that I saw them when I brought that bucket of water. That's all. I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you saw between 10 and 15, you mean Bosniaks, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the entrance to the hangar, close to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd quoted transcript from this trial, page 7095, a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you stand by what you said, you heard two short bursts of fire and the shooting occurred about five minutes later?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That night of the 13th, the second night after St. Peter's Day, Petrovdan, started quietly, there was no shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure. There were two explosions, strong explosions, two or three, a bit earlier, that I heard, but I don't know anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that you heard those explosions in the afternoon and not in the night?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact time, but I think it was towards the evening, towards dusk, those two or three strong explosions that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you again that there is another version of these events, according to which when the night fell shooting occurred from infantry weapons and after a short lull, hand grenades were thrown through the windows into the warehouse where the prisoners were held, that's transcript 699 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that and I don't know anything about those hand grenades. If somebody threw them, it may have been from the other side that I couldn't see. I wasn't even close.
