utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, page 45, line 5, the page quoted was 6999, and an additional two lines are on page 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at P01563, a Prosecution exhibit? While we are waiting, let me say that this is a photograph of the Kravica warehouse that we have seen in this courtroom before. You saw this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the centre of this structure, you see four openings without doors.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you at any point in those few days, on the 12th or the 13th, see any Bosniaks, Muslims, in that part of that building?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Just before that, I know that there were some burned-down machines, trucks and tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those machines and tractors, did they occupy all that space?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: This open hangar, it was almost full, almost full of those machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you testified before the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and some of that testimony has already been quoted back to you - you said, amongst other things, that among those specials you did not see an officer or somebody who could be taken as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see anybody. I didn't see a commander. I didn't see what the commander was like. I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, I was quoting from transcript that we received from the Prosecution, P02188, page 42 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 28 in the English version. I will repeat the number. This is Exhibit number P02818, page 41 in the B/C/S version and page 28 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, sir, you saw the two specials, as you called them, who were in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you see maybe two or three more?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the road towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally did not see any other specials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the night when you stood guard, together with Zoran Eric, they were replaced, they were replaced by some others?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was at midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those whose shift had ended were fair, they treated you well, and they treated the prisoners well?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. I don't know how they treated the prisoners. The person who was there, he asked for some water, when I brought it I saw that they were calm, peaceful, like lambs, and the other, I didn't -- wasn't able to talk to. I couldn't talk to him. There was nothing to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again I've been warned that in the transcript, your words have been recorded differently. Who said to you that the prisoners were calm?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The person whom I gave the bucket of water. I thought that he was a special. I don't know who he was. I only know that he was not a local, he was not from our village. Judging by his accent and everything else he was not a local.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You know Ilija Nikolic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the brother of your then-director, Jovan, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Nikola Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Gajic? Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those few days, did you see the two of them in the warehouse in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Ilija before that. He arrived with Jovo to the -- to the farm where we were, and later on, I also saw him when he arrived in Kravica. As for Gajic, I don't remember ever seeing him there. Maybe he did arrive but I didn't see him because I was not there 24 hours a day. I had things to do, things to tend to. I didn't stand guard to see who would arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from stories that you heard later on that Ilija Nikolic was there at that place at the time when the incident happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not clear on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us in clarifying the role of some other persons, the roles that these people possibly had in these events? If I were to tell you that during that time in front of the warehouse, providing security for the prisoners, was also a person whose name is Milo Obradovic, also known as Riba, that together with two other men, in front of the entrance door to the warehouse, he put up a table and interviewed the prisoners looking for those who knew anything about the attack on Kravica on the 7th of January 1993? Would you agree with me that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I am only going to tell you about Milo Obradovic, also known as Riba, that I knew him well. He killed -- he was killed in a traffic accident. He was no longer alive. I know that he brought a crate of beer on one day. Whether it was for himself or not, I don't know. A special asked him whether there was any beer to be had and he said, "I have it." And the special asked where it is and he says, "In the car."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you was whether you saw him by a desk at the entrance to the Kravica warehouse where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him. I can't say that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also you did not see who the dead soldier was and you were not sure whether he was the same soldier to whom you had given water?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I only heard that the person that I had given water to, but I didn't come closer to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You only heard it from your colleague, Miladin Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that. I don't know who had told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, let us look at another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is 4D -- P01892. P01892. While we are waiting for this document in e-court, I would like to tell you that this is the book called the protocol of the health centre in Bratunac. Could we please look at the page 30 in B/C/S and page 2 in the English version? We've already had an occasion to see that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid whether he would be able to read it. Try your best, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honours. I'll try to make it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see for yourself that this is a protocol. Mr. Djukanovic, since you can't see it I still wanted to ask you something. In this protocol of the health centre in Bratunac, on the 1489, it says, on the 13th of July 1995, at 1730 hours, a person was brought to the health centre in Bratunac, he was a member of the Red Beret unit, he had been wounded in Kravica, and his name was Milisav Stanojevic or maybe Miroslav Stanojevic, we will establish that later, and he had a gunshot wound or wounds described here in. My question to you is this: Do you know anybody by the name of Miroslav or Milisav Stanojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Milisav is my best man, Milisav Stanojevic. He is still alive but barely because he is disabled, if we are talking about him. As for Miroslav, I don't know anybody by that name. Milisav had been wounded in the leg. For 12 years he hasn't been able to walk and if you're talking about him, that's my best man and my neighbour and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that your best man was not born in 1972, that he is a bit older?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure when he was born but I believe he is older.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How old is your best man today? Maybe I should ask you this, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that his brother -- actually, he has two brothers older than him. One is the same age as me. The other was born in 1952 and Milisav is younger than the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's finish with this. Are you familiar with this Red Beret unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that on the strength of the Bratunac Brigade there was a Red Beret unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I only heard that that existed in Belgrade and that they still exist in Belgrade, the Red Berets and in our local midst I never saw them, I never understood anything about them. But I didn't go there that much to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukanovic. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I have one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple questions, Mr. Djukanovic. Could I just look at exhibit -- the one we just looked at, the Bratunac hospital record. 4DP01892. Mr. Djukanovic, you were read just the first line from this hospital record. Could you scroll over, please? I want to read the next two for you. If we can scroll to the left for Mr. Djukanovic so he can see the beginning. Records 1490 and 1491, both 13 July 1995, the first one, 13 July, 1995 at 1740, Rade, son of Milan, Suteric [phoen], if we scroll over, after his birth-date, we see in the next column, Sekovici and his unit is "MUP special brigade", place of wounding, "Kravica", burns on the palms of his hand. Did you hear any more about what kind of wounding happened to the wounded special in Kravica that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: The one who was wounded, he was wounded through the chest. And another gunshot wound through one of his arms. That's what I heard. I did not see it myself. I just heard stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The next one, 1491, 13 July 1995 at 1900, Krsto Dragicevic, from Skelani Special Police, Skelani his unit, wounded in Kravica, deceased.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJUKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing else, then, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukanovic, that concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that there are two IC documents on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those would be just the two photo stills of Kravica marked by the witness. PIC00114 and PIC00115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there would be no opposition to those from the Defence? Mr. Stojanovic you'd like to tender any exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender 4D107 for admission. This is the list of members of the R Battalion issued by the Ministry of Defence, the Bratunac Division, on the 10th of July 1995. And as for the other exhibits, I believe that I've only used those that have already been either tendered or admitted, so there is no need for me to retender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 107 or 157? 107, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be admitted but that list was not translated yet. So they will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Prost wanted to check that the Prosecution exhibits were included in them. Yes. Shall we bring in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trivic. If you could kindly read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do we need a Rule 90 warning?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, in these circumstances, I don't think one will be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it's your witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I was born in a village in Bosanska Gradiska municipality, which is in the territory of the present-day Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I identify myself as a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do for the next few moments, sir, is review with you your military service history. And if I make any mistakes or if there is anything you'd like to clarify please feel free to do so as I move through it, okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You completed the command staff academy in 1971 and became a professional soldier in the JNA serving in Slovenia until 1988?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I completed the military academy, not the command staff academy. It was a military academy which I completed after the secondary school and that was in 1971. From then to 1988, I served in various garrisons in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you later served in Belgrade as an instructor in the high military academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. After the military academy, I completed the military staff academy, the post-graduate studies of military skills and that education allowed me to apply to be a teacher at the military academy. I was given the job in 1988. I arrived at the centre in Belgrade. I was involved with the tactics department at the military academy, and it was at the military academy where I taught military tactics up to 1990 and then in 1990 I was appointed as the head of that year's class, that started education at the military academy in that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Let's see if I can get this right. Beginning in January of 1993, you served as the chief of staff of the 1st Guards based in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1993, I joined the army of Republika Srpska and was appointed chief of staff of the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade that was established then in January as a unit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you served in the guards until approximately August of 1994, when you took command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was chief of staff at the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you took command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, you took over from then Colonel Radislav Krstic, who himself then became Chief of Staff to the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took over duty from the then commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, Colonel Krstic, who was going on to become Chief of Staff at the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You commanded the 2nd Romanija Brigade and if we can refer to it just as the Romanija Brigade to shorten it a little bit, through the Srebrenica and Zepa operations and you were injured in the Zepa operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were on medical leave until the end of June 1996?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in treatment for 11 months. That's when I was on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then reported to the 1st Corps in Banja Luka and served as commander of an infantry brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that treatment, I was appointed to the garrison, the Banja Luka garrison, and I became commander of one infantry brigade in the Banja Luka garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in approximately 1997, you also served as commander of an artillery unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask Mr. Thayer to speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After being commander of an infantry brigade, there occurred reorganisation in the army and that unit ceased to exist and my specialisation is actually artillery officer so I became commander of the mixed artillery regiment, also in the Banja Luka garrison, in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you subsequently served as assistant commander for morale and legal affairs in the corps at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A year or 18 months later, I became assistant commander of the 1st Corps for morale, political and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you retired with the rank of Colonel in 2002, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the duty from which I retired in 2002 as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were called and testified as a Prosecution witness in the Blagojevic trial in February of 2004 and then you returned as a Defence expert witness in June of 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In the Blagojevic case, I started as a Prosecution witness, with my own consent, in February 2004, and again with my consent and at the request of the Defence counsel, since it was not possible to conduct the cross-examination, the Chamber allowed my engagement as a witness and consultant for the Defence in June 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I think as I've mentioned to you before, you're not being called as an expert here. I just want to ask you some questions about your activities on the ground during the time period in which you served in the Srebrenica and Zepa operations, okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber where the 2nd Romanija Brigade was headquartered?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Romanija brigade was stationed in a place called Knezena [phoen] in Sokolac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just roughly describe the geographical boundaries for which your brigade was responsible? If it's easier to refer to some surrounding locations, please do so, we don't need a detailed explanation but generally, sir, if you would?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The defence lines in the defence area of the brigade were focused on defence from Kladanj-Olovo direction, and I believe that the structures, features that were the boundaries of the forward line of defence were in Krivojevic village. That's the Niksic plateau and they were linked up with units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and that line then went towards the enemy up to a feature called Slivanj in Han Pijesak municipality. Of course, because of the layout of the terrain, that line went outside of normal rules of brigade organisation. It was a very long line, therefore, over 50 kilometres, covering three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the strength of your brigade, in terms of overall personnel, both combat and support services, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean the total number in the unit, in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In itself, since it was a motorised brigade, it originated from the JNA with the envisaged establishment equipment. It was well equipped with over 4.000 personnel assigned to all the duties that were envisaged by establishment and manning all the equipment the brigade had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I want to turn your attention to late June, early July, of 1995. With respect to the Srebrenica operation, did you receive any particular order informing you to prepare for an action?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In end June or maybe beginning of July, I can't remember the exact date now, I received a preparatory order in the brigade command to make a selection and form a unit for active duty, active operations, and these men had to be picked out of my units and prepared for engagement outside the brigade's area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from whom was that order issued and in what form was it issued, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The order was issued by the corps commander. It is his privilege to issue orders. And it was a preparatory order based on an evaluation of the situation in the corps, the command issued such orders to all the units, including my brigade, to prepare my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, at this time, we are speaking about General Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the corps commander was General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what specifically did you do in response to that order, in terms of forming this unit for active duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: According to normal procedure, I studied the order, consulted my co-workers and commanding officers in the command, and prepared assignments for subordinate units, to prepare the personnel, which is ready and which they evaluate to be capable of performing tasks outside the zone of the brigade, together with the logistical support, that is younger and abler men. And of course, after that, they had to be pulled out of their units from the lines on which they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in pulling these soldiers and resources away from your brigade to form this combat group, if I may call it that, how did you ensure that the brigade would be able to continue to carry out its own mission, duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: My main approach and the approach of my command and other officers, who participated in the decision-making, is not to harm the combat readiness of any unit, any battalion in doing so and to pull out one platoon from each battalion and no battalion should be considerably affected by the absence, temporary absence, of one platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how many soldiers approximately all together did your combat group contain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Sometime -- in fact somewhere in my documents I have the exact number but I believe that combat group was around 200 men, including me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that also include the rear services personnel as well or is that actual combat individuals?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The entire group, including me, down to the last soldier who was engaged in the logistical support of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you told the approximate size of this combat group that you were supposed to constitute?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember very clearly, but in view of our strength, it was the equivalent of a strong infantry company reinforced with a platoon of tanks, which I remember arrived to that area after they received their assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what other specific weaponry elements did this combat group contain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: There were three tanks. That's one tank platoon that I mentioned. And from each battalion, one infantry platoon was taken. Two mortars. And the rest was infantry weapons carried by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Other than the mortars, did you take any other artillery or heavy weaponry with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you assign someone to command this combat group?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assigned and stipulated in my own order that the commander of that combat group would be my operations officer, Major Ljubo Eric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point did you then receive an order to move your unit, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did it instruct you to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It was ordered that this unit should arrive on the 5th of July in the morning to the area of Zeleni Jadar, that it should deploy there and await further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you follow that order, sir, and if so, did your combat group arrive at the appointed time in the Zeleni Jadar area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came on time, and awaited further orders there, and I conveyed to them those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you based in any particular location in the Zeleni Jadar area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That is a small population centre, Jasenova village. I classified it as a village. And that's where my forward command post of the brigade for that task was established, including the commander of that combat group, myself and all the other organs involved in the combat group assigned from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point after you arrived, together with your combat group, at that location, did you receive an order personally to report anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The combat group marched on its own and I received an assignment to report to Pribicevac area on the 5th, where I received specific tasks stipulating the axes of action. I was briefed and oriented as a person coming from a different area. We got areas where reconnaissance was to be conducted. We were given axes along which to act. And in the afternoon of the 5th, the other commanders received their instructions and their specific orders within the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom did you report, sir, at Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Krstic, or General Krstic, I think he was already general by that time, who led the reconnaissance in the stage of preparation for that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the Pribicevac area. Was there some sort of command post based there, and if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber what it was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: From the way things developed later, I knew of course that the forward command post of the Drina Corps was there, but I and the others did not participate at the forward command post. We were instead at a topographic feature which provided a good vantage point of the area where the units would be engaged in the future, so we were not actually at the command post but at a point, at a feature from which we were able to orient ourselves in that area and see the axes of future action. It was actually an observation point where -- from which we could see various roads, various structures, communications, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to other commanders receiving their instruction. Which other brigades do you recall participating in this operation? And if you would, when you refer to the brigade, if you could also refer to the name of the commander of the brigade as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In that operation, mainly involved were parts of the brigades which had defence areas within the corps's area, and only the Romanija Brigade was an exception. It had nothing no do with Srebrenica or Zepa until then. So there was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Mr. -- or rather Colonel Pandurevic, I believe the commander of the Milic Brigade was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I just may interrupt you, sir, you identified according to the transcript the commander of the Bratunac Brigade being Colonel Pandurevic, just wanted to make sure I didn't read that wrong.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not Bratunac. The commander of the Bratunac Brigade -- which transcript do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm looking at my live transcript of your answer, sir. That's what I'm referring to. So I just wanted to make sure that I didn't read it wrong. If you would just please start over and if you can recall the brigades that were involved in this operation and the commanders of those brigades?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Involved in the operation were the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic was its commander; the Zvornik Brigade commanded by Colonel Pandurevic; the Milic Brigade commanded by Captain First Class or Major Nastic; the Bircanska Brigade commanded by Colonel Andric; and the Skelani Independent Battalion led by Colonel Vukota, I believe. I think Vukota was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple follow-up questions, sir. You referred to the Skelani Independent Battalion. The name suggests something. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber to what entity that battalion is attached?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That battalion, as the name says, was an independent battalion within the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm again looking at my transcript and I'm not seeing the name of the brigade that you identified as being commanded by Colonel Andric. Can you just say that again for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Bircanska Brigade from Sekovici, its command was in Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir was that also referred sometimes as the Birac Brigade, and as the 1st Sekovici Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the brigade, Sekovici Brigade or Birac Brigade, from the Birca area. That's the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you're at this observation point. As you sit here today, can you recall which of these commanders you personally saw there at that time, if any?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: In my previous interviews and statements, I've explained that I remember, and that I've also recorded for myself - I did it in a notebook that I always carried on me - I mostly recorded those that were my next-door neighbours, whose activities depended on mine and vice versa, and as for Colonel Pandurevic, since we were neighbours in carrying out our tasks, and when I say neighbours, I mean our units were next to each other, he was there, I'm sure. As for the others, whether they were on that observation point, I can't say whether they were there personally or they had delegated their group commanders or something. I wouldn't be able to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see it's time for a break, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, before we continue with the movements of your combat group. I just wanted to follow up --?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I could hardly hear you. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll get closer to the microphone. Okay, that's better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now we can hear you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to go back to a couple of answers you gave, and I know it's been 12 years since these events. I know you've spent a long time here since you've been here reviewing all of your prior statements and testimony, you've met with a number of teams, including meeting with myself. So I just want to make sure that we are getting your best recollection about certain events. You testified just before the break that your recollection was that the strength of your combat unit was approximately a strong company. Do you recall your testimony on this subject in the Blagojevic case involving what the strength of your numbers were, the strength of that combat group? It's not a major point but I just want to make sure that we are getting your best recollection. Do you recall what you said on this issue in Blagojevic and if you don't, if my reading you your answer help refresh your recollection, I can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I assume that when I said that I meant an equivalent of the battalion. If this is what you mean, then, yes, that was the case as far as I remember. When I was preparing for this, and as I was studying the materials that I had, the strength of a unit can be given almost to the last soldier. And when you take that into account, and when you ponder on that, then it would not be even 50 per cent of a battalion. That's why I've used the term "strong company". Hence the difference. There is no other difference. I still adhere by what I have stated before. Since I was given some other units. But here I'm talking about my strength, from the brigade, not the original strength that I had under my command originally. The total strength you have in my materials that you have used, that you have at your disposal, my original was reinforced by some troops that equalled a battalion. No longer the strong company that I had from my brigade. If you want me to, I can give you the material that I have consulted but that you already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, sir. I appreciate that. And do you recall whether the order you received required a battalion strength unit to be formed? Or was it some other unit that you were asked to form? And if you don't recall, that's fine. I just want to find out what your best current recollection is.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The unit that I was supposed to command, I don't know exactly what it says in the preparatory order, but I know that it should have been a combat group and that all together, the whole strength that I had under my command equalled a battalion before I could say that it was something of a strong company that I had received from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The second issue I just wanted to revisit with you briefly is the location -- the actual location of this first meeting that you had when you reported to General Krstic on the 5th. You've described being at an observation location in the area of the Pribicevac IKM. Do you recall what you testified to in Blagojevic - and this is at page 7474, in case anybody is looking at the English - with respect to where you had your first briefing with General Krstic? Again it's not a major issue. I just wanted to make sure we are getting your best recollection on this, sir. And if you like, I can read you the answer that you gave in the Blagojevic case to that question.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The first oral report or debriefing on the unit leaving the area of responsibility was at the command position of the Bratunac Brigade. Nobody ever asked about the place where the task was issued. To this very day I have never been asked where that task was actually implemented. And as for the final task and the report on the unit leaving, its strength, what we had at our disposal, that report, that debriefing, was at the command post of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So just so we are clear, did you -- do you recall ever reporting to General Krstic at the actual Bratunac Brigade headquarters itself in Bratunac, as opposed to anywhere else out in the field on the 5th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: But of course, of course. That's what I'm saying. Before the tasks were given where the activities were supposed to start, we had to report as to how many men we had in every unit that had arrived in the territory from which they would be deployed into combat. That was the combat -- the command position of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac. That's where I submitted my briefing. I received tasks about the beginning of attack. As for the rest, that was at the observation point in the general area of the forward command post in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you went to Pribicevac after reporting to the command headquarters in Bratunac, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we were briefed even before that. We were given the situation, the deployment, the strength of the forces, and then at the command post we were given the beginning of attack order, we reported on the strength of the unit. We did everything that is customarily done before any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at the observation point that you were discussing just prior to the break, you told us that you recall seeing Commander Pandurevic there. Do you recall seeing any other Drina Corps officers at that location at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, and according to the customary procedure, there was also the intelligence man from the Drina Corps, who was there, who briefed us about the situation and the estimates of the situation on the enemy side. He also gave us an estimate of their strength, deployment, according to what he knew, according to the intelligence that he had. He was an officer whom I had not seen before. There was also Colonel Vicic who gave us the task. He was the operations guy. Who else? I don't remember who else was there but these two were certainly there. That's how I have recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this intelligence officer with the corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I learned later on that I believe that he was Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. I don't know his name but his family name was Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any Main Staff officers at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about any MUP officers, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've already discussed the general subject matter of this briefing and meeting. Did you receive any further orders, specific orders, while were you there, and, if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Where? At the observation point or at the command post in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's start with the observation point. Were you given any specific orders at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: At the observation point, before the beginning of the task, what is usually given, and that's why we met there on that occasion, axes, the estimated deployment, and lines of defence on the axes of activity, an estimate of the strength of the enemy on the lines, what can be expected, where the artillery devices are. This is the procedure which is undertaken in every situation before you start preparing for the implementation of the task, before you start moving the units into offensive, and also what is given are the lines that are expected to be achieved at the end of the task. This is the procedure that is regulated by the rules for the operation of staffs, commands, units, everything that is prescribed as a procedure which allow the officers to orientate themselves before the task and prepare their units for the estimated situation and what lies ahead, what can be expected. These are tasks that are usually recorded and spelled out in any combat order or attack order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you given a combat-readiness date, sir, that is a date by which the forces would be ready to go into action?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was given in Bratunac. Whatever was not supposed to be dealt with on the ground was dealt with in Bratunac at the command post when we received the attack order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that combat-readiness date, sir? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 6th of July, I believe; not that I believe, I know that the 6th of July was specified as the combat-readiness date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the main objective, as you understood it, of this operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The main objective of the operation that was set out by the corps command as a result of the events of the previous months -- years and months, that preceded this decision, was to separate the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica, in view of the fact that there were constant incidents, sabotage actions from the protected zones and losses were suffered both on the lines and in the villages that were in the immediate vicinity of the protected areas. And the tasks of the units were geared towards that general task and that's how the task was spelled out. And from that general task, all the other tasks arose, and this also influenced the implementation of the commitment that the Muslim side had taken on two years before and the task was the commitment was to demilitarise those zones in order to allow the two peoples to live normally. That was my understanding of the task. And the objective of those offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a minor correction in the transcript. The answer was not recorded on page 17 [as interpreted], line 20, page 70, line 12, the witness said sabotage and terrorist actions. And the only thing that we have recorded in the transcript is sabotage actions. The terrorist actions were omitted from the transcript. Maybe the witness could repeat that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask Colonel Trivic whether he can confirm this. Did you say sabotage and terrorist action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did part of the objective of separating the two enclaves also involve in any way affecting the size of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: With the very separation and entry of units into that interspace between enclaves, that were held anyway by the units of VRS, the Skelani Battalion and part of the Milici Brigade, with the very separation, a certain effect was created on the territory of those protected areas because it's precisely from that territory that I won't say under the protection but under the shield of UNPROFOR units, UNPROFOR points, incursions had been made before, against our units. And all the actions that do not target the army are considered to be terrorists, because it was not only soldiers that were on those lines but mainly the civilian population. That's why I characterised this, that's the way I understood it, that these were sabotage actions, terrorist acts, where people doing work in their yards, in their fields, would be killed, their throats would be slit, they would be robbed, and left to rot. So these units had the task to separate the enclaves and that implied a narrowing down of the territory in which they were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So do I understand your answer correctly, sir, then, that a component of the objective of this operation was to reduce the size of the enclaves themselves, in addition to separating them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: First came the separation, and from that follows automatically a narrowing down of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, for clarity's sake, when the Prosecutor asked "reducing the size", is he referring to the population size or the area geographically?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank my friend for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I presume we've been understanding each other that we are talking about the geographical size of the enclaves, not the numbers of the population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any recollection as to the size to which your army was planning to reduce these enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, after these briefings on the 5th of July, did you return to your base in Jasenova and if so, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I left that meeting and went to the IKM in the area of Jasenova and conveyed to the commanding officers their respective tasks. I notified them of their respective missions related to the beginning of the operation, the introduction of units on various axes, the method of execution of these tasks, and methods of support in the way that is normal when you convey to various units and their commanders the tasks received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I note that you've taken out what I believe is your diary that I've furnished to my friends, and it's perfectly appropriate if you need to, to refer to it in answer to some of my questions or the questions of my colleagues or the Trial Chamber, but I would ask that, unless you absolutely have to, if you could put it to the side so that we all understand that when you're answering a question that it's coming from your memory and if you do need the aid that we know for the record when you're getting the aid, okay? Thank, sir. Now, without going into too much detail, Zeleni Jadar is to the south of Srebrenica, Jasenova is located where in respect to Zeleni Jadar, just orient us north, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You're right, Zeleni Jadar is to the south, but Jasenova is in the immediate vicinity of what is known as Zeleni Jadar, as it is marked on the map, and it's in the immediate vicinity on a plateau. There are several houses of Jasenova village where my units were deployed, and the forward command post that had the task of performing command in the execution of these tasks. Relative to Zeleni Jadar, Jasenova is to the west, one or two kilometres to the west. But you could also say it is south to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the axis of attack for your combat group, just in terms of directionally, sir, first, and then if you can give us some towns or locations, villages, that would help orient us, please do so. Again we don't need a whole lot of detail but just generally.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I have already dealt with these questions more than once and reminded myself, so it's Jasenova village, Kiprovo, Slapovici, Zivkovo Hill, Bojna, Stupina. All of these are rather geographic features or settlements on that axis or otherwise prominent features that were laid out along that line, and are to the west of my unit's position and the settlement of Srebrenica. You could say that it was a kind of axis for the engagement of my unit in active combat, that was a reference point to determine the axis of engagement of my unit. Those are the features that I remember. If you want more detail I would have to refresh my memory but I think this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The direction, just roughly, is north-northwest from your position in Jasenova, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, from your position facing your axis of attack, did you have any brigade formations or neighbours to your right? And if so, what was it? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: My neighbour to the right was a part of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say a part of the Zvornik Brigade, do you recall whether that part was a particular unit and, if so, was it commanded by anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: There were units from the Zvornik Brigade led by Major Jolovic, also known as Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what the name of his particular unit was, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: That usual name was used, in view of their importance and their experience and their readiness for executing missions, they had an unusual name, the Drina Wolves, I believe that was the full name of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was your neighbour to the left, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: My neighbour to the left was a unit from the 1st Birac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to move things along, if I can, you had a date of 6 July for combat readiness. But is it fair to say that not much happened until the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: As far as my unit was concerned, on that particular axis, there was no action, nothing was started because the conditions were bad, the fog was very dense. I just reported that visibility was very poor. If we engaged in combat, we would get lost, and there were no prominent features to help us orient ourselves so we didn't start anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please describe the terrain on your axis, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean the configuration of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, just the nature of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Hilly, mountainous, hilly terrain, with features that are suitable for taking up positions and making fortifications but very difficult for offensive actions because you would need very well-trained forces to get anywhere near defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on 9 July, were you in fact able to begin advancing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of July, parts of my unit moved to attack in typical military movement, with offensive reconnaissance, as we call it in the military, and we wanted to see how ready the enemy forces were, how well they organised their defence, and then we were supposed to mount an attack in the area of Kiprovo village. As far as I remember, it was an area occupied by the cemetery of that village, at a mountain pass, at elevation, and when we emerged there, we got a view of the slope, and from that point on, it was much easier to make decisions and decide on further lines of movements for the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you advanced, did you reach some sort of refugee settlement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in this careful movement, we reached a refugee settlement that we were aware of. It's called Slapovic. By that time, there were no longer even occasional shootings from the other side, from the enemy side, and we saw in that settlement prefab houses probably donated by some foreign organisations, and the Muslim population. It was the middle of the day when we got there and realised there was no fire from that settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw any people in the settlement at that time? Or had it been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It was abandoned. There were no people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And along your group's axis, were there any UN observation posts, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: On my axis, on my unit's axis, there were no observation points.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that, I believe, other than some mortars, your combat group did not bring any artillery or heavy weaponry with it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No, only two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall shelling during this period of time and over the next couple of days, either in your area or within ear-shot of your position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Not that I recall. All the fire was from the mortars that I had, 82 millimetres, and 100, 200 metres ahead of my forces, one or two shells were dropped to see if any forces would emerge in response, but we didn't see any forces in position on the line of our movement, nor did we see any casualties. I didn't see and I don't remember any other fire, any other shelling, especially not large calibre. I suppose I would have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any fixed military targets that you were provided with on any kind of list or that you became aware of on your axis?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't given anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, you spent the night of 9 July back at your base in Jasenova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to keep things moving along, bringing you up to the 10th of July, were you redirected in any way at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: You mean with my unit or on my own?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your unit, sir. Was your unit -- did your unit or yourself receive any orders to redirect your unit on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received the assignment to continue along the axis towards Stupina which was a small adjustment because the axis that had been given the brigade, the northwestern part of the territory relative to Srebrenica and we were told to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay of the I thank you, sir. We'll stop on 10 July, I think, for the time being, if we may, Mr. President, we do have one brief scheduling matter that we've been in contact with our friends about that we would like to bring to the Chamber's attention in just a couple of minutes, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Trivic, we are going to adjourn for the day with your evidence. We'll resume at 9.00 on Monday. In the meantime, if -- I would like to advise you not to discuss your evidence with anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand and I'm familiar with that from my previous visits and cautions I received earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Mr. Thayer, you're going to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I may just wait until the witness leaves. Mr. President, we are constantly looking at the witness schedule and the time estimates. Given the pace at which this week and today has unfolded, given the length of cross-examination that's estimated for the current witness, and particularly given the fact that we have the Defence intercept expert scheduled for next Wednesday and Thursday as fixed days, we are really going to try to, I think, complete that beginning -- begin and complete that testimony in two days. We are going to have to withdraw the witness who is currently scheduled to follow the current witness. I believe he's Witness 102, Mr. Salapura. I think we are going to have to send him home because we simply are not going to have any realistic chance of completing his testimony before the intercept operator begins to testify. I think that this current witness, given the time estimates, may take us well enough into Tuesday so that calling Mr. Salapura will inevitably involve having to break up his testimony, potentially in the early part, and then bring him back, who knows when. He's already been here for a bit of time. We've consulted with as many of our friends as we could over the break and that we just wanted to advise the Court of that significant change in the schedule and I'll incorporate that into the usual scheduling memo that I send out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you in the position to tell us how long are you going to -- you are going to stay with this current witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to do my best it try to move it along faster. I think it's going to be probably an hour more with him. Things will pick up. We are about to enter Srebrenica and I think things will pick up a little bit. It may be more than an hour but I think I can do the remaining testimony in an hour, and then we've got, as I understand it, over four hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I'd like to ask the Defence, whether they would stand by with their estimate tendered earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy to go first, Your Honour. Mr. Krgovic is going to cross-examine the witness but we wrote to the court officer earlier this week to say we would take rather longer with this witness than we had originally planned. Mr. Krgovic's present estimate is 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was simply going to say that we've been alive to this issue since the last break when we all got together. There has been quite a good deal of e-mail correspondence on the length of cross-examination, and everybody is doing their very best to be as accurate as possible and I think the current estimates add up to something like five hours, and I have, I think, the authority to say that everybody is doing their very best to say that that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Five hours in total?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. So I think Mr. Thayer is quite right, it will take us to the end of Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that Defence is, in general, happy with the suggestion of Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn for the week and resume on Monday at 9.00. Please have a nice weekend, everybody.
